'''Jerzy Maria Michał Łoś''' ({{IPA|pol|ˈjɛʐɨ ˈwɔɕ|lang}}; born 22 March 1920 – 1 June 1998) was a Polish [[mathematician]], [[logician]], [[economist]], and [[philosopher]]. He studied at the [[University of Lviv]], and during his career held positions at several institutions including the [[University of Wrocław]], the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]] and the [[University of Warsaw]]. 

He is noted for his contributions to [[model theory]] (particularly [[Łoś's theorem]]), [[mathematical logic]], [[abelian group|Abelian group theory]], and [[mathematical economics]]. In the late 1940s, he introduced some of the first systems of [[Temporal logic|temporal]] and [[epistemic logic]].<ref>{{cite journal | last= Parol | first= Aleksander | title= The Influence of Jerzy Łoś on Early Developments in Temporal Logic | journal= Studia z Historii Filozofii | volume= 11 | issue= 3 | year= 2021 | pages= | doi= 10.12775/szhf.2020.020 | publisher= Nicolaus Copernicus University}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1= Kupś | first1= Tomasz | last2= Jarmużek | first2= Tomasz | title= The Heritage of Jerzy Łoś’s Philosophical Logic and the Polish Question | journal= Studia z Historii Filozofii | volume= 11 | issue= 3 | year= 2020 | publisher= Nicolaus Copernicus University | doi= 10.12775/SZHF.2020.026}}</ref>

==Life and career==
Łoś was born on 22 March 1920 in [[Lwów]] (now [[Lviv]], Ukraine) in the [[Second Polish Republic]] as the son of Zygmunt, a Doctor of Law, and Zofia ({{nee|Roztworowska}}), a landowner and social activist.<ref name="MatHist">{{cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Los/ |title=Jerzy Maria Michał Łoś |author=J.J. O'Connor, E.F. Robertson |work=MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive |access-date=11 August 2026}}</ref> In 1937, he matriculated at the [[Jan Kazimierz University]] (now the [[University of Lviv]]), where he initially studied medicine before switching to philosophy and chemistry.<ref name="MatHist"></ref> 

During [[World War II]], Łoś worked as an official at a sugar factory in [[Lublin]]. After the war, he pursued his studies in philosophy at the [[Maria Curie-Skłodowska University]] in Lublin. In 1946, influenced by the writings of [[Jan Śleszyński]], he published ''An Attempt to Axiomatise Traditional Logic'' in which he examined [[traditional logic]], particularly the laws of [[immediate inference]] on the basis of relations between extensions of arguments. The following year, he received a master's degree on the basis of his work ''Analiza metodologiczna kanonów Milla'' (The Foundations of a Methodological Analysis of Mill's Method).<ref name="MatHist"></ref> 

In 1947, Łoś relocated to [[Wrocław]], where he worked as an assistant at the Faculty of Physics and later the Faculty of Logic of the [[University of Wrocław]]. Inspired by [[Hugo Steinhaus]] and [[Edward Marczewski]], he started developing a greater interest in mathematics. In 1949, Łoś obtained his [[doctorate]] based on his dissertation ''O matrycach logicznych'' (On Logical Matrices) written under the supervision of [[Jerzy Słupecki]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=146375 |title=Jerzy Łoś |website=Mathematics Genealogy Project |access-date=11 August 2026}}</ref> In the same year, he became a member of the Real Functions Group at the [[Institute of Mathematics of the Polish Academy of Sciences|Institute of Mathematics]] of the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="MatHist"></ref>

In 1952, Łoś started working at the [[Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń|Nicolaus Copernicus University]] in [[Toruń]] and was appointed head of the Group of Algebra of the Institute of Mathematics.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Balcerzyk |first1=Stanisław |last2=Bartol |first2=Wiktor |last3=Orłowska |first3=Ewa |last4=Wieczorek |first4=Andrzej |last5=Wojciechowska-Waszkiewicz |first5=Agnieszka |title=Jerzy Łoś 1920-1998 |journal=Studia Logica |volume=65 |issue=3 |year=2000 |pages=301–314 |doi=10.1023/A:1005253713004}}</ref> He earned his [[habilitation]] there in 1955. In 1961, Łoś continued his academic career at the [[University of Warsaw]] where he shifted the focus of his research from [[foundations of mathematics]] and [[algebra]] to [[applied mathematics]], [[game theory]] and [[economics]].<ref name="MatHist"></ref> He held positions in three institutes there: first the Institute of Philosophy, then the Institute of Mathematics and finally the Institute of Computer Science.<ref name="Pacholski"></ref> 
In 1967–1994, he sat on the editorial board of ''[[Fundamenta Mathematicae]]''.<ref name="NePach">Ludomir Newelski, Leszek Pacholski, "Jerzy Łoś (1920–1998)", ''Fundamenta Mathematicae'', vol. 170 (2001), pp. 1–10.</ref> In 1969, he served as acting president of the [[Polish Mathematical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.impan.pl/images/prezentacja70w3f.-przytycki.pdf |language=pl |title=Instytut Matematyczny PAN na przestrzeni 70 lat |trans-title=The Institute of Mathematics of the PAN over the Span of 70 Years |website=impan.pl |author=Feliks Przytycki |access-date=11 August 2026}}</ref> 

In 1974, Łoś was awarded the Knight's Cross of the [[Order of Polonia Restituta]].<ref name="ELWS"></ref> In January 1976, Łoś was among the signatories of the ''Memorial 101'', a protest letter of Polish intellectuals to the Extraordinary Commission of the [[Sejm]] opposing the proposed amendments to the [[Constitution of the Polish People's Republic]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Kultura |journal=Kultura |issue=3 (342) |year=1976 |location=Paris |page=30}}</ref> In 1983, he became a full member of the Polish Academy of Sciences, and in 1984, he joined the [[Warsaw Scientific Society]].<ref name="ELWS">{{cite web|url=https://encyklopedia.slw.uw.edu.pl/articles/los-jerzy-maria-michal/ |language=pl |title=ŁOŚ, Jerzy Maria Michał |author=Aleksandra Gomułczak, Anna Brożek, Jacek Jadacki |work=Encyclopaedia of the Lwów-Warsaw School |date=1 October 2025 |access-date=11 August 2026}}</ref> In 1986, he received the {{ill|Sierpiński Medal|pl|Medal im. Wacława Sierpińskiego}} conferred jointly by the University of Warsaw and the [[Polish Mathematical Society]]. In 1995, he accepted an [[honorary doctorate]] from the [[University of Hagen]], Germany.<ref name="MatHist"></ref>

During his career, Łoś visited such institutions as [[University of California at Berkeley]] (where he conducted a seminar on model theory with [[Alfred Tarski]]), [[Aarhus University]], [[Institut Henri Poincaré]], [[Yale University]] and the [[University of Wisconsin]].<ref name="MatHist"></ref>

In 1996, Łoś suffered from a severe [[stroke|brain stroke]]. He was thenceforward ill until his death in 1998 in Warsaw.<ref name="Pacholski">{{cite web|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-symbolic-logic/article/in-memoriam-jerzy-los-19201998/781064CD85BEBD578CD716068FEE03A6 |title=In Memoriam: Jerzy Łoś 1920-1998 |author=Leszek Pacholski |work=The Bulletin of Symbolic Logic |date=20 July 2016 |access-date=12 August 2026}}</ref>

===Contributions===
[[File:Jerzy Los caricature.png|thumb|220px|Jerzy Łoś caricature by Leon Jeśmanowicz, 1953]]
His 1947 master's thesis ''Analiza metodologiczna kanonów Milla'' (The Foundations of a Methodological Analysis of [[Mill's methods|Mill's Method]]) is regarded as pioneering in the field of [[temporal logic]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Łoś|first=Jerzy |url=http://dlibra.umcs.lublin.pl/dlibra/doccontent?id=4085|title=Podstawy analizy metodologicznej kanonów Milla |journal=Zasoby Biblioteki Głównej Umcs |date=1947|publisher=nakł. Uniwersytetu Marii Curie-Skłodowskiej |language=pl}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Rescher |first1=Nicholas |last2=Urquhart |first2=Alasdair |title=Temporal Logic |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=Vienna |year=1971 |page=12 |isbn=978-3-211-80995-2}}</ref> [[Arthur Prior]] references Łoś's work in his principal book on temporal logic, having learned about it through a review by [[Henryk Hiż]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hiż |first=Henry |title=Review of: Jerzy Łoś, ''Podstawy analizy metodologicznej kanonów Milla'' |journal=The Journal of Symbolic Logic |volume=16 |issue=1 |year=1951 |pages=58–59 |doi=10.2307/2268676}}</ref>

In 1954, Jerzy Łoś and [[Robert Lawson Vaught]] independently established that a first-order theory having only infinite models is [[complete theory|complete]] if it is [[categorical theory|categorical]] in some infinite cardinal greater than or equal to the cardinality of its language. It is now referred to as the [[Łoś-Vaught test]] and its applications include demonstrating that the theory of closed  [[first-order logic]] formulas true on the [[Rado graph]] is complete.<ref>{{cite book |last=Marker |first=David |title=Model Theory |series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics |volume=217 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=New York |year=2002 |isbn=0-387-98760-6 |page=42}}</ref>

He is especially known for his work in [[model theory]], in particular for [[Ultraproduct#Łoś's theorem|Łoś's theorem]] (also known as the Fundamental Theorem on Ultraproducts), which states that any [[first-order formula]] is true in an [[ultraproduct]] if and only if it is true in "most" factors.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%C5%81o%C5%9B+ultraproduct+theorem |title=Łoś ultraproduct theorem |website=ncatlab.org |access-date=11 August 2026}}</ref> His conjecture on the [[categorical theory|categoricity]] of countable theories, later proved by [[Michael D. Morley]], and in its uncountable form by [[Saharon Shelah]], played a crucial role in stimulating the development of [[stability theory]], which became a major branch of model theory.<ref name="NePach"></ref>

In model theory, he also proved many preservation theorems, including the [[Łoś–Tarski preservation theorem]], which asserts that the set of formulas preserved under taking [[Substructure_(mathematics)|substructures]] is exactly the set of ''universal'' formulas.<ref>{{citation | first1=Wilfrid | last1=Hodges | author-link=Wilfrid Hodges | title=A Shorter Model Theory | publisher=Cambridge University Press | isbn=0521587131 | year=1997 | page=143}}</ref> 

He also gave significant contributions, as well, to [[foundations of mathematics]], [[Abelian group|Abelian group theory]] and [[universal algebra]]. In the 60's he turned his attention to [[mathematical economics]], focusing mainly on production processes and dynamic decision processes.
